259-ballads-of-a-cheechako:
Robert W. Service follows his Yukon success with ballads of newcomers to the North. Ballads of a Cheechako, from the American 1909 edition, addresses the man of the high north in rough, rolling rhyme. Cheechako means tenderfoot, and Service's speakers learn the country hard.

The Ballad of the Northern Lights, the Black Fox Skin, Pious Pete, and Blasphemous Bill fill the contents. Burials, bargains, and dance-hall loves mix humor with cold truth. Service's verse keeps the gold-rush North alive in memory. The book pairs with his Spell of the Yukon.
ballads-of-a-cheechako:
Robert W. Service, the Scottish-born bank clerk turned Yukon poet, gathered Ballads of a Cheechako in 1909, following the wild success of his first book of Klondike verse. A cheechako is a newcomer to the North, a tenderfoot learning the gold country the hard way. Service gives such men, and the old sourdoughs who mock and teach them, a set of rollicking tales in rhyme.

The ballads ride through trail camps, dance halls, frozen creeks, and claims, mixing jokes with sudden death and homesick longing. Service writes in strong, swinging lines meant to be read aloud, and he does not hide his love for the rough North. The book helped make him one of the best-selling poets of his day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-isidor-:
Franz Isidor Proschko, born at Hohenfurt in Bohemia on 2 April 1816 and died at Vienna on 6 February 1891. He was an Austrian author in the public service, whose writings always breathed a Catholic spirit. His most important works include books for the young, Leuchtkäferchen in 1849 and Feierstunden in 1854, and historical romances in two volumes each. They include Hollenmaschine in 1854, Der Jesuit in 1857, Die Nadel in 1858, and Pugatschew in 1860. Selected tales and poems followed in 1873.

His complete works were edited in six volumes between 1901 and 1909 by his daughter Hermione, born at Linz in 1851. She was herself a distinguished Catholic writer of poems, Heimatklange, tales under firs and palms, a book from Austria's laurel grove, and novels of joy and sorrow under God's guidance. The entry presents father and daughter as a literary family serving Catholic letters in Austria, Proschko himself spending a life divided between government departments and the writing desk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julian-klaczk:
Julian Klaczko was a Polish author and diplomat of Jewish birth who became a leading French voice. Born at Vilna in 1825, he took a doctorate at Königsberg in 1847, worked under Gervinus at Heidelberg, and protested the incorporation of Posen into the German Confederation. Ruined by his father's losses, he moved to Paris in 1850 and lived by his pen.

Baptized after his father's death, Klaczko wrote brilliant French essays and, with Kalinka, edited the Polish News against rash uprisings. His 1862 study of the poet Krasinski fixed his French fame, and his Etudes de diplomatie of 1866 sharply judged the Powers over Denmark and Poland. He died at Cracow in 1906.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tadeusz-kosci: Tadeusz Kosciuszko was the hero of Poland. This entry traces his Saratoga, his Maciejowice, and his fame. The engineer of two revolutions: his patriot sword crowned Saratoga in the 1777 of the Congress in the field of the old Hudson.
podcast-joerogan-3uKe5AoPKKo:
Former CIA officer Mike Baker talks with Rogan in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience about the UFO whistleblower claims that hit Congress and the news. Baker spent years in covert work before moving into private security, and he judges such claims with a spy's habits.

He weighs what a real disclosure would look like against what the public has actually been shown. Rogan pushes on crash stories, hidden programs, and why officials speak in careful hints. Baker answers with tradecraft logic: who benefits, what can be checked, and what stays fog. The segment is a cool-headed take on a hot story.
podcast-tuckercarlson-3EAYlgYB2ko:
Tucker Carlson devotes this episode to the deep past as his guests and sources describe it. The subjects include giants in old accounts and the pyramids of Egypt. They also include the CIA's documented experiments with psychic spies, and civilizations said to be more advanced than the modern world before some great fall.

Each topic has a paper trail of some kind, from declassified remote-viewing files to nineteenth-century newspaper reports of giant skeletons. Carlson treats them as pieces of one suppressed history. The claims vary widely in support, and the episode moves by suggestion as much as by proof. It is preserved as a specimen of a popular genre: alternative history argued at length for a mainstream-sized audience. Listeners can enjoy the tour while keeping their own tally of what is documented and what is not.
the-tragedy-of-the-korosko:
Arthur Conan Doyle opens The Tragedy of the Korosko by explaining why the public never read of it in the papers. Personal and political reasons held the story back, though versions leaked into a provincial paper and were discredited. Doyle says the narrative was collated from the sworn statements of Colonel Cochrane Cochrane and the letters of Miss Adams of Boston. Captain Archer of the Egyptian Camel Corps added evidence given before a secret inquiry at Cairo.

The Korosko herself, a turtle-bottomed stern-wheeler of thirty-inch draught, left Shellal on 13 February 1895 bound for Wady Halfa. Doyle prints her passenger card: colonels, Bostonians, a Frenchman, a Dublin couple, and a Birmingham clergyman. This documentary frame gives his Nile adventure the flavour of a suppressed scandal about to be told at last.
